title: Agentic AI 2026
lines: Agentic AI 2026 explains why useful agents need more than an intelligent model.
The surrounding software turns model predictions into actions with real consequences.
The book follows tools, memory, permissions, verification, and recovery as one engineering problem.
Its argument is that autonomy needs boundaries matched to the work being delegated.
You will learn to compare agent designs through evidence, control, and total operational cost.
The later proposals matter because the earlier chapters establish how to judge them.

title: From answers to actions
lines: Imagine an agent helping with a customer’s request for a refund.
It reads a public page, then proposes returning the customer’s money.
Those operations need different permissions, even within the same task.
Permission to read should not silently become permission to pay.
The surrounding software must check each proposed action against its own rules.
This distinction makes the book’s question concrete: who controls the consequences?

title: Follow the trajectory
lines: The book then compares ways to organize a sequence of uncertain decisions.
An agent might alternate reasoning and action, or work from an explicit plan.
Verification adds another question: did the proposed step produce the intended result?
Memory preserves useful state, but also creates material that later decisions may trust.
Multiple agents introduce coordination costs alongside their possible division of labor.
These patterns become useful reading when compared against the same task and failure conditions.

title: State can mislead
lines: A public page can contain instructions that the user never authorized.
An agent might read those words while collecting information for its task.
Storing them as trusted instructions carries the error into later decisions.
The book examines this security problem across tool results, context, and memory.
Source labels and action checks help distinguish retrieved content from authorized instructions.
These failure cases explain why a longer memory can also preserve mistakes.

title: Inside the harness
lines: The harness is software that mediates between a proposed action and execution.
For our refund, it checks the tool, arguments, permissions, and required approval.
An instruction found on a webpage cannot supply that missing authority.
Meanwhile, the agent can continue permitted work, such as assembling supporting information.
The book connects these controls to checkpoints, budgets, monitoring, and recovery.
Its account helps readers inspect a system beyond its framework name.

title: Count the whole cost
lines: Once the boundary is visible, the economic comparison also changes.
The book counts tool calls, retries, supervision, and failures alongside model usage.
A cheap individual response may belong to an expensive, unreliable trajectory.
A constrained workflow may outperform broader autonomy for a predictable recurring task.
The argument is comparative, not a rule that one pattern always wins.
Readers gain a way to discuss efficiency without hiding the human work around automation.

title: Bounded generality
lines: Those comparisons lead to the book's tension between flexibility and dependable control.
Hardcoded workflows can be predictable while struggling with changing or unfamiliar tasks.
Unrestricted autonomy can adapt while making behavior and cost harder to bound.
The book explores intermediate designs that preserve choice within explicit operational limits.
This is an engineering tradeoff to measure, rather than a slogan about maximum independence.
It prepares readers to evaluate the concrete runtime proposals in the final movement.

title: Proposals under test
lines: The later chapters present ScriptaHubAgentLib and a proposed runtime called MRP-VM.
These designs explore skill execution, controlled context, state, and responsibility within agent systems.
Their inclusion does not establish that they outperform every existing agent architecture.
The book instead describes evaluation questions and limits that could challenge their value.
That distinction separates reading an engineering proposal from accepting a product claim.
Return to the earlier failure and cost chapters when judging what these proposals add.

title: Read with a task
lines: Start with a task where an agent could take a consequential wrong step.
Read the opening architecture chapters to identify its state, permissions, and recovery needs.
Then use the pattern comparisons and cost discussion to examine plausible alternatives.
The final research agenda asks what evidence would justify greater autonomy.
Agentic AI 2026 is valuable as a connected argument about accountable delegation.
Read it to decide which freedoms your system needs, and which boundaries make them usable.
